Reference: McCrary (2008)

Model Setting

The regression discontinuity (RD) design identifies a treatment effect at a cutoff if the conditional expectations of the counterfactual outcomes are continuous in the running variable. When the assignment rule is public knowledge, agents who want the treatment may adjust the running variable, and this manipulation (sorting) can make those conditional expectations discontinuous. The paper gives the analogy of a doctor who randomizes heart patients into waiting rooms A and B and plans to give the statin to room A: if patients learn the rule and walk to room A, randomization is undone, and room A becomes crowded. The RD analogue of the crowded room is a discontinuity at the cutoff in the density of the running variable, with surprisingly many units just qualifying for a desirable treatment and surprisingly few just failing to qualify.

The paper proposes a density test: a Wald test of the null hypothesis that the discontinuity at the cutoff in the density of the running variable is zero. The estimator extends the local linear density estimator of Cheng, Fan and Marron (1997) and has two steps: a finely gridded histogram, and local linear smoothing of the histogram separately on each side of the cutoff. The paper proves that the estimated log discontinuity is consistent and asymptotically normal, gives a standard error, proposes an automatic choice of binsize and bandwidth, and reports Monte Carlo evidence. Two applications follow. For popular elections to the U.S. House of Representatives sorting is neither expected nor found (log discontinuity −0.060-0.060−0.060 with standard error 0.108), and for roll call votes in the House sorting is both expected and found (0.521 with standard error 0.079). The test complements the usual check that predetermined characteristics are smooth at the cutoff, and it can always be carried out because it needs only the running variable. It is informative when manipulation is monotonic, and a continuous density is neither necessary nor sufficient for identification without auxiliary assumptions.

Identification and Manipulation

Let YiY_iYi​ be an outcome and DiD_iDi​ a binary treatment:

Yi=αi+βiDi=α+βDi+εi(1)Y_i=\alpha_i+\beta_iD_i=\alpha+\beta D_i+\varepsilon_i \tag{1}Yi​=αi​+βi​Di​=α+βDi​+εi​(1)

In counterfactual notation αi=Yi0\alpha_i=Y_{i0}αi​=Yi0​ and βi=Yi1−Yi0\beta_i=Y_{i1}-Y_{i0}βi​=Yi1​−Yi0​. Treatment is assigned on the basis of the running variable RiR_iRi​. Underlying RiR_iRi​ is an unobservable index Ri0R_{i0}Ri0​, the running variable that would obtain if there were no program, and the running variable is manipulated when Ri≠Ri0R_i\neq R_{i0}Ri​=Ri0​. The identification results of Hahn, Todd and Van der Klaauw (2001) are interpreted as holding for the unobservable index. The maintained assumption (A0) is:

E[αi∣Ri0=r],E[βi∣Ri0=r]andfRi0(r)are continuous in r(2)E[\alpha_i|R_{i0}=r],\quad E[\beta_i|R_{i0}=r]\quad\text{and}\quad f_{R_{i0}}(r)\quad\text{are continuous in }r \tag{2}E[αi​∣Ri0​=r],E[βi​∣Ri0​=r]andfRi0​​(r)are continuous in r(2)

where fRi0(r)f_{R_{i0}}(r)fRi0​​(r) is the density of Ri0R_{i0}Ri0​. This is enough for an RD estimator based on Ri0R_{i0}Ri0​ to identify a local average treatment effect, and it is slightly stronger than the Hahn-Todd-Van der Klaauw conditions because it adds continuity of the density. Without manipulation (the program is announced at the same time as it is implemented, or agents do not care about assignment) the assumption holds with RiR_iRi​ in place of Ri0R_{i0}Ri0​. With manipulation, E[αi∣Ri=r]E[\alpha_i|R_i=r]E[αi​∣Ri​=r] and E[βi∣Ri=r]E[\beta_i|R_i=r]E[βi​∣Ri​=r] can be discontinuous at the cutoff although E[αi∣Ri0=r]E[\alpha_i|R_{i0}=r]E[αi​∣Ri0​=r] and E[βi∣Ri0=r]E[\beta_i|R_{i0}=r]E[βi​∣Ri0​=r] are continuous.

Two kinds of manipulation are distinguished. Under partial manipulation the running variable is under the agent's control but also has an idiosyncratic element, which typically does not create an identification problem (an admission index combining test scores and grades, or a union certification vote by secret ballot). Under complete manipulation the running variable is entirely under the agent's control, which typically does create one (an employer choosing 14 employees to stay below a legal threshold of 15, or a grader misreporting a pre-test score). Lee (2008) shows that identification survives partial manipulation if the conditional density fR∣W(r∣w)f_{R|W}(r|w)fR∣W​(r∣w) is continuous in rrr, where WWW denotes unobserved types: every type then has the same chance of a draw just above and just below the cutoff. This is not directly testable, but it implies that the conditional expectation of any baseline characteristic is continuous in the running variable, which is the standard specification check, and it also implies that the density fR(r)f_R(r)fR​(r) of the running variable is continuous, which is the basis of the density test.

The density test may be uninformative unless the program moves the running variable in one direction only. Manipulation is monotonic if:

Ri≥Ri0 for all iorRi≤Ri0 for all i(3)R_i\geq R_{i0}\ \text{for all }i\qquad\text{or}\qquad R_i\leq R_{i0}\ \text{for all }i \tag{3}Ri​≥Ri0​ for all iorRi​≤Ri0​ for all i(3)

Two hypothetical examples about summer school assigned by a test score show what can go wrong. In the first, the average treatment effect is zero, summer school helps half of the students and harms half, and teachers push the scores of those who would be helped and barely passed below the cutoff and the scores of those who would be harmed and barely failed above it. The estimated effect is positive, but the manipulation is not monotonic and the two flows are equally numerous, so the density stays continuous and the test fails to detect the problem. In the second, teachers give bonus points to some students who barely fail and subtract points from nobody; the density becomes discontinuous, but if the students who receive points are chosen at random an average treatment effect is still identified.

A Job Training Example

A simple labour supply model shows how manipulation arises and what it does. Agents maximize the present discounted value of utility from income over two periods and choose full-time or part-time work in each period. Part-time work means supplying a fraction fif_ifi​ of full-time labour and receiving the fraction fif_ifi​ of full-time income; the fraction differs across workers and is set by the employer before period 1. Period 1 earnings and eligibility for a job training program that takes place between the periods are:

Two-Step Estimator

Traditional histograms and kernel estimates that smooth over the cutoff give neither a point estimate nor inference for the discontinuity, and a kernel estimator applied separately to each side is badly biased at the boundary. The local linear density estimator corrects boundary bias, is 100 percent efficient among linear estimators in a minimax sense at a boundary point (Cheng, Fan and Marron 1997), and its first step is of interest in its own right, as the analogue of the local averages shown with RD regression estimates. The first step is a very undersmoothed histogram whose bins never contain points on both sides of the cutoff ccc. It is the frequency table of a discretized running variable:

g(Ri)=⌊Ri−cb⌋b+b2+c∈{…,c−5b2,c−3b2,c−b2,c+b2,c+3b2,c+5b2,…}(9)g(R_i)=\left\lfloor\frac{R_i-c}{b}\right\rfloor b+\frac{b}{2}+c\in\left\{\ldots,c-5\frac{b}{2},c-3\frac{b}{2},c-\frac{b}{2},c+\frac{b}{2},c+3\frac{b}{2},c+5\frac{b}{2},\ldots\right\} \tag{9}g(Ri​)=⌊bRi​−c​⌋b+2b​+c∈{…,c−52b​,c−32b​,c−2b​,c+2b​,c+32b​,c+52b​,…}(9)

where ⌊a⌋\lfloor a\rfloor⌊a⌋ is the greatest integer in aaa and bbb is the binsize. Observations with Ri=cR_i=cRi​=c fall in the bin c+b/2c+b/2c+b/2, which is appropriate if ties are assigned to treatment. The proposition of the paper is as follows. Let f(⋅)f(\cdot)f(⋅) be a density that has three continuous and bounded derivatives everywhere except at ccc, let KKK be the triangle kernel, and suppose h→0h\to0h→0, nh→∞nh\to\inftynh→∞, b/h→0b/h\to0b/h→0 and h2nh→H∈[0,∞)h^2\sqrt{nh}\to H\in[0,\infty)h2nh​→H∈[0,∞). If R1,R2,…,RnR_1,R_2,\ldots,R_nR1​,R2​,…,Rn​ is a random sample with density f(r)f(r)f(r), then:

nh(θ^−θ)→dN(B,245(1f++1f−))(16)\sqrt{nh}\left(\hat{\theta}-\theta\right)\xrightarrow{d}N\left(B,\frac{24}{5}\left(\frac{1}{f^{+}}+\frac{1}{f^{-}}\right)\right) \tag{16}nh​(θ^−θ)d​N(B,524​(f+1​+f−1​))(16)

where the asymptotic bias is:

B=H20(−f+′′f+−−f−′′f−)(17)B=\frac{H}{20}\left(\frac{-f^{+\prime\prime}}{f^{+}}-\frac{-f^{-\prime\prime}}{f^{-}}\right) \tag{17}B=20H​(f+−f+′′​−f−−f−′′​)(17)

and f+′′f^{+\prime\prime}f+′′, f−′′f^{-\prime\prime}f−′′ are the right and left limits of the second derivative of the density at ccc. The estimator converges at the nonparametric rate nh\sqrt{nh}nh​, its variance is larger where the density is low on either side of the cutoff, and its bias depends on the difference in the relative curvature of the density on the two sides. The implied approximate standard error is:

σ^θ=1nh245(1f^++1f^−)(18)\hat{\sigma}_\theta=\sqrt{\frac{1}{nh}\frac{24}{5}\left(\frac{1}{\hat{f}^{+}}+\frac{1}{\hat{f}^{-}}\right)} \tag{18}σ^θ​=nh1​524​(f^​+1​+f^​−1​)​(18)

and the test of continuity compares θ^/σ^θ\hat{\theta}/\hat{\sigma}_\thetaθ^/σ^θ​ with the standard normal distribution. If the bandwidth is of order n−1/5n^{-1/5}n−1/5, the rate that minimizes the asymptotic mean squared error, then H>0H>0H>0 and the normal distribution is not centred at zero: a confidence region built with the standard error above covers the probability limit of θ^\hat{\theta}θ^ well, but not θ\thetaθ. The two remedies in the literature are to estimate the bias, which requires yet another bandwidth, and undersmoothing, which the paper adopts: take a reference bandwidth and divide it by 2.

Binsize and Bandwidth Selection

For a fixed bandwidth the estimator is robust to the binsize provided that h/b>10h/b>10h/b>10, say. The reason is visible in the decomposition:

The paper prints the left-hand side of this expression as E[f^+−f+]E[\hat{f}^{+}-f^{+}]E[f^​+−f+] and the leading term in braces as h2tj2f′′+h^2t_j^2f^{\prime\prime+}h2tj2​f′′+, without the factor 12\frac{1}{2}21​; the form above is the one consistent with the appendix, where the bias of f^+\hat{f}^{+}f^​+ is −h212110f+′′-h^2\frac{1}{2}\frac{1}{10}f^{+\prime\prime}−h221​101​f+′′. Since the tjt_jtj​ are b/hb/hb/h apart, the sum is a Riemann approximation to an integral whose height is dominated by the h2h^2h2 term because h>bh>bh>b. Good performance of θ^\hat{\theta}θ^ therefore does not require a careful choice of binsize.

It does require a good choice of bandwidth. The paper regards visual inspection of the first-step histogram and the second-step smoother under several choices of bbb and hhh as probably the best method: superimposing the smoother on the scatterplot (Xj,Yj)(X_j,Y_j)(Xj​,Yj​) reveals at once the likely consequence of a different bandwidth. Cross-validation and the plug-in selector of Cheng (1997) are less subjective, but the plug-in method needs integrals of squared density derivatives that are particularly hard to estimate at a boundary. The paper's recommendation is subjective choice guided by an automatic procedure, with the deviation from the automatic value reported. The automatic procedure has two steps. First, compute the first-step histogram with the binsize:

b^=2σ^n−1/2(28)\hat{b}=2\hat{\sigma}n^{-1/2} \tag{28}b^=2σ^n−1/2(28)

where σ^\hat{\sigma}σ^ is the sample standard deviation of the running variable. Second, fit a global fourth-order polynomial to the histogram separately on each side of the cutoff, compute for each side:

κ[σ~2(b−a)∑f~′′(Xj)2]1/5,κ≐3.348(29)\kappa\left[\frac{\tilde{\sigma}^2(b-a)}{\sum\tilde{f}^{\prime\prime}(X_j)^2}\right]^{1/5},\qquad\kappa\doteq3.348 \tag{29}κ[∑f~​′′(Xj​)2σ~2(b−a)​]1/5,κ≐3.348(29)

and set h^\hat{h}h^ equal to the average of the two quantities. Here σ~2\tilde{\sigma}^2σ~2 is the mean squared error of the polynomial regression, b−ab-ab−a is the length of the fitted range (XJ−cX_J-cXJ​−c on the right and c−X1c-X_1c−X1​ on the left; in this expression bbb is not the binsize), and f~′′(Xj)\tilde{f}^{\prime\prime}(X_j)f~​′′(Xj​) is the second derivative implied by the polynomial. This is the rule-of-thumb selector of Fan and Gijbels (1996), with a constant κ\kappaκ that is specific to the triangle kernel at a boundary.

Monte Carlo Evidence

Each design has 1000 replications and four rules: (A) basic binsize and basic bandwidth from the automatic procedure, (B) basic binsize and half the basic bandwidth, (C) half the basic binsize, (D) twice the basic binsize. The true density is continuous in every design, so the reported size is the rejection rate of a true null.

  • Design I: 50,000 draws from a normal distribution with mean 12 and standard deviation 3, the distribution of Ri0R_{i0}Ri0​ in the job training example. Under rule A (bbb of 0.027, hhh between 1.45 and 1.56) the bias of θ^\hat{\theta}θ^ is −0.0064-0.0064−0.0064, its standard deviation 0.0353, the mean of the proposition standard error 0.0345, and the size of the t-test 0.063. Halving the bandwidth (rule B) lowers the bias to −0.0018-0.0018−0.0018 and raises the standard deviation to 0.0513 (mean standard error 0.0489, size 0.060). Rules C and D give biases of −0.0063-0.0063−0.0063 and −0.0066-0.0066−0.0066 and sizes of 0.064 and 0.060, so the binsize hardly matters.

  • Design II: the same distribution with only 1000 observations. Rule A gives bias −0.0420-0.0420−0.0420, standard deviation 0.1800, mean standard error 0.1763 and size 0.058; rule B gives bias −0.0059-0.0059−0.0059, standard deviation 0.2564, mean standard error 0.2532 and size 0.043; rules C and D both have size 0.067.

  • Design III: 10,000 observations from a 75-25 mixture of normals with means 0 and 4 and variance 1, with the cutoff at 2, just to the left of a local minimum where the density is strongly quadratic. Rule A gives bias 0.0252, standard deviation 0.1598, mean standard error 0.1484 and size 0.065; rule B gives bias 0.0011, standard deviation 0.2079, mean standard error 0.2010 and size 0.056; rules C and D have sizes 0.061 and 0.069.

  • Conclusions: the bias is small and falls as the bandwidth shrinks, undersmoothing nearly eliminates it, the proposition standard error tracks the true sampling variability, and tests have size between about 4 and 7 percent. Normal Q-Q plots of the t-statistics show a good fit far into the tails, with neither skewness nor fat tails.

Empirical Applications

  • Popular elections to the U.S. House, 1900-1990: in the incumbency study of Lee (2001, 2008) incumbency is assigned discontinuously at 50 percent of the vote. Complete manipulation is unlikely, because voters cannot coordinate and democratic safeguards limit fraud. The running variable is the Democratic margin, the vote share of the Democratic candidate less the largest vote share of any other candidate, in contested elections with a Democratic candidate (nnn of 16,917), so that the Democrat wins if and only if the margin is positive. With b=0.004b=0.004b=0.004 and h=0.02h=0.02h=0.02 (the automatic procedure selects b=0.004b=0.004b=0.004 and h=0.13h=0.13h=0.13, which oversmooths at the mode) the density looks smooth near zero, and θ^=−0.060\hat{\theta}=-0.060θ^=−0.060 with standard error 0.108, so continuity is not rejected.

  • Roll call votes in the U.S. House, 1857-2004: here coordination is expected. Votes are a repeated game, each representative's vote is public, so commitments and vote trading are credible, and the size principle of Riker (1962) implies that the bills most likely to reach the floor are those expected to pass narrowly. The running variable is the fraction voting in favour (nnn of 35,052), with b=0.003b=0.003b=0.003 and h=0.03h=0.03h=0.03 (automatic: b=0.0025b=0.0025b=0.0025 and h=0.114h=0.114h=0.114). In the first-step histogram, passage by 1-2 votes is 2.6 times more likely than failure by 1-2 votes. The estimate is θ^=0.521\hat{\theta}=0.521θ^=0.521 with standard error 0.079, a t-ratio of 6.6. The estimate is, if anything, slightly attenuated, because a few bills require a supermajority and their cutoff is not observed.

  • Interpretation: the majority rule in the House should not be viewed as generating quasi-random assignment of policy decisions, whereas the electoral application passes the test. In both cases the first-step histogram shown together with the smoother conveys how sensitive the estimate is to the smoothing choices.

References

  • McCrary, Justin. 2008. “Manipulation of the Running Variable in the Regression Discontinuity Design: A Density Test.” Journal of Econometrics, 142(2): 698–714.

This is the potential-outcomes model written as a random-coefficient regression. YiY_iYi​ is the outcome and Di∈{0,1}D_i\in\{0,1\}Di​∈{0,1} the treatment. The intercept αi=Yi0\alpha_i=Y_{i0}αi​=Yi0​ is the outcome unit iii would have without treatment and the slope βi=Yi1−Yi0\beta_i=Y_{i1}-Y_{i0}βi​=Yi1​−Yi0​ is its own treatment effect, so both differ across units. The second equality only adds and subtracts the population means α=E[αi]\alpha=E[\alpha_i]α=E[αi​] and β=E[βi]\beta=E[\beta_i]β=E[βi​]:

Yi=α+βDi+(αi−α)+(βi−β)Di⏟εiY_i=\alpha+\beta D_i+\underbrace{(\alpha_i-\alpha)+(\beta_i-\beta)D_i}_{\varepsilon_i}Yi​=α+βDi​+εi​(αi​−α)+(βi​−β)Di​​​

The error εi\varepsilon_iεi​ therefore contains both heterogeneity in levels and heterogeneity in gains, and it is correlated with DiD_iDi​ whenever units with unusual αi\alpha_iαi​ or βi\beta_iβi​ are more likely to be treated. A comparison of treated and untreated means gives

E[Yi∣Di=1]−E[Yi∣Di=0]=E[βi∣Di=1]+{E[αi∣Di=1]−E[αi∣Di=0]}E[Y_i|D_i=1]-E[Y_i|D_i=0]=E[\beta_i|D_i=1]+\left\{E[\alpha_i|D_i=1]-E[\alpha_i|D_i=0]\right\}E[Yi​∣Di​=1]−E[Yi​∣Di​=0]=E[βi​∣Di​=1]+{E[αi​∣Di​=1]−E[αi​∣Di​=0]}

so the term in braces is selection bias. The RD design removes it by comparing units with running variable just above and just below the cutoff, which works only if E[αi∣Ri=r]E[\alpha_i|R_i=r]E[αi​∣Ri​=r] and E[βi∣Ri=r]E[\beta_i|R_i=r]E[βi​∣Ri​=r] are continuous there; that requirement is stated for the unmanipulated index in equation (2), and the same outcome equation is used in the job training example of equations (4) to (8).

This is the maintained assumption (A0) of the paper. It is stated for Ri0R_{i0}Ri0​, the running variable that would obtain if the program did not exist, and not for the observed RiR_iRi​. The first two parts say that the average untreated outcome E[αi∣Ri0=r]E[\alpha_i|R_{i0}=r]E[αi​∣Ri0​=r] and the average gain E[βi∣Ri0=r]E[\beta_i|R_{i0}=r]E[βi​∣Ri0​=r] change smoothly with the latent index: units just on either side of any point rrr are comparable. These are the Hahn-Todd-Van der Klaauw conditions. The third part, continuity of the density fRi0(r)f_{R_{i0}}(r)fRi0​​(r), is an addition, and it is what makes a density test meaningful: without the program there is no reason for the population to bunch on one side of ccc.

If treatment were assigned on Ri0R_{i0}Ri0​, say Di=1(Ri0≥c)D_i=1(R_{i0}\geq c)Di​=1(Ri0​≥c), then by equation (1)

lim⁡r↓cE[Yi∣Ri0=r]−lim⁡r↑cE[Yi∣Ri0=r]=E[βi∣Ri0=c]\lim_{r\downarrow c}E[Y_i|R_{i0}=r]-\lim_{r\uparrow c}E[Y_i|R_{i0}=r]=E[\beta_i|R_{i0}=c]r↓clim​E[Yi​∣Ri0​=r]−r↑clim​E[Yi​∣Ri0​=r]=E[βi​∣Ri0​=c]

which is a local average treatment effect. The assumption is weak because it concerns a world without incentives to sort. The whole point of the paper is that (A0) can hold while the same statements fail for RiR_iRi​: when Ri≠Ri0R_i\neq R_{i0}Ri​=Ri0​ for some units, E[αi∣Ri=r]E[\alpha_i|R_i=r]E[αi​∣Ri​=r], E[βi∣Ri=r]E[\beta_i|R_i=r]E[βi​∣Ri​=r] and fR(r)f_R(r)fR​(r) may all jump at ccc. The simulated example after equation (8) satisfies (A0) exactly and still produces such jumps. Under monotonic manipulation, equation (3), a jump in fRf_RfR​ is the observable symptom, measured by θ\thetaθ in equation (13).

The definition says that the program moves the running variable in one direction only: either nobody ends up with RiR_iRi​ below the value Ri0R_{i0}Ri0​ it would have had without the program, or nobody ends up above it. The direction must be the same for all units.

Why it matters: the density test looks at the net flow of mass across the cutoff. Suppose treatment is desirable and given when Ri≥cR_i\geq cRi​≥c. Under monotonic manipulation with Ri≥Ri0R_i\geq R_{i0}Ri​≥Ri0​, units can only cross ccc from the left to the right, so the density of RiR_iRi​ just below ccc falls and just above ccc rises:

lim⁡r↓cfR(r)>fRi0(c)>lim⁡r↑cfR(r)\lim_{r\downarrow c}f_R(r)>f_{R_{i0}}(c)>\lim_{r\uparrow c}f_R(r)r↓clim​fR​(r)>fRi0​​(c)>r↑clim​fR​(r)

and θ\thetaθ of equation (13) is nonzero. Without monotonicity two opposite flows can cancel. In the first summer-school example, the mass pushed down across ccc equals the mass pushed up across ccc, the density stays continuous, and yet the composition on the two sides differs, so the RD estimate is biased while the test has no power. The triangle kernel puts weight 111 at distance zero and lets the weight fall linearly to 000 at distance one bandwidth; with argument t=(Xj−r)/ht=(X_j-r)/ht=(Xj​−r)/h a bin receives weight 1−∣Xj−r∣/h1-|X_j-r|/h1−∣Xj​−r∣/h if it is within hhh of the evaluation point and zero otherwise. This is the first step of the automatic procedure: a rule for the binsize of the histogram. σ^\hat{\sigma}σ^ is the sample standard deviation of the running variable, so b^\hat{b}b^ is in the units of RiR_iRi​ and scales with its dispersion, and nnn is the sample size. The rule is a convention, not the solution of an optimization problem; what matters is its rate. Since b^\hat{b}b^ shrinks like n−1/2n^{-1/2}n−1/2 while a bandwidth of the mean-squared-error-optimal order shrinks like n−1/5n^{-1/5}n−1/5,

b^h∝n−1/2+1/5=n−3/10→0\frac{\hat{b}}{h}\propto n^{-1/2+1/5}=n^{-3/10}\to0hb^​∝n−1/2+1/5=n−3/10→0

so the condition b/h→0b/h\to0b/h→0 of the proposition (equation (16)) holds automatically, and by equation (27) the estimate is insensitive to the exact value of bbb. The bins are nevertheless not empty: the expected count in a bin is nb^f(Xj)=2σ^f(Xj)nn\hat{b}f(X_j)=2\hat{\sigma}f(X_j)\sqrt{n}nb^f(Xj​)=2σ^f(Xj​)n​, which grows with nnn; for a normal density at its mode this is about 0.8n0.8\sqrt{n}0.8n​.
